title: Skidmore v. Swift & Co.
lead: Seven Swift employees spent several nights each week near the plant’s fire hall, free to sleep or amuse themselves but required to answer alarms. Their overtime suit asked whether that restricted waiting counted as work and how much weight a court should give the federal administrator’s guidance.

actors.name: Seven Swift & Company employees
actors.role: Fort Worth packing-plant workers seeking compensation for nighttime on-call periods.

actors.name: Swift & Company
actors.role: Employer that provided fire-hall accommodations and paid separately for alarms.

actors.name: Administrator of the Wage and Hour Division
actors.role: Federal enforcement official who urged reversal as a friend of the Court.

actors.name: Justice Jackson
actors.role: Author of the Supreme Court’s single opinion.

proceedings: The district court treated nighttime inactivity as nonwork as a matter of law and denied recovery; the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded for a factual inquiry, without fixing compensable hours or awarding money.
limits: The Administrator’s proposed division of sleeping, eating, and other on-call hours was not a binding Court determination. The case predates the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946. The source reports no post-remand award.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Daytime employees agree to remain available at night
sections.cue: What restrictions and payments defined the arrangement?
paragraphs: Seven employees at Swift & Company’s Fort Worth packing plant worked five days a week from 7 a.m. until 3:30 p.m., with a half-hour lunch excluded. Two maintained the fire hall and firefighting equipment; others operated elevators or supplied relief for fire duties. They received weekly salaries, and nobody disputed that the daytime duties were working time.

An oral agreement also required them to stay in the company fire hall or within hailing distance three and a half to four nights each week, ready to respond to alarms. Swift supplied heated and air-conditioned accommodations, sleeping quarters, games, and a radio. The men could sleep or amuse themselves but could not freely leave the vicinity. Apart from answering alarms, the stipulated facts described no required nighttime task.

No fires occurred during the relevant period. Alarms were rare, generally required no more than an hour, and brought a separate payment of fifty cents, later increased to sixty-four cents. Whether the surrounding waiting time also required compensation became the dispute.

sections.title: The lower courts exclude the waiting as a matter of law
sections.cue: Why was the Supreme Court asked to reopen the inquiry?
paragraphs: The employees sued under the Fair Labor Standards Act for approximately $77,000 in overtime compensation, liquidated damages, and attorneys’ fees. The district court accepted the stipulated facts but made no separate factual determination whether the nighttime arrangement constituted work in whole or part. It instead concluded as a matter of law that pleasurable activities and personal chores were not work, and denied the entire claim. The Fifth Circuit affirmed.

In the Supreme Court, the parties favored broad all-in or all-out treatment of the inactive periods. The Administrator of the Wage and Hour Division, the federal official responsible for enforcing the Act, appeared as a friend of the Court urging reversal. The Administrator proposed excluding sleeping and eating time while including other on-call hours. The Court had to address both the proper employment inquiry and the weight due that administrative view.

sections.title: The Court rejects a categorical answer about inactivity
sections.cue: What must the factfinder learn about this particular employment?
paragraphs: Justice Jackson wrote the Court’s single opinion. The companion decision in Armour established that waiting time could qualify as work under the Act. But that principle did not supply an automatic rule for every inactive-duty arrangement.

The factfinder needed to examine the agreement, the parties’ conduct in carrying it out, the nature of the service, the relationship between service and waiting, and the surrounding circumstances. A worker could be hired to wait or could instead wait for employment to begin. Pay might cover waiting and active tasks together or only the active tasks. Lodging might facilitate performance or be part of compensation. The actual relationship mattered, including circumstances the parties had not expressly anticipated.

Recreational amenities made the restriction less unpleasant without eliminating the restriction on freedom. Conversely, being on call did not make every hour compensable automatically. The special payment for alarms distinguished this arrangement from Armour and required its own assessment. Each case had to turn on its facts.

sections.title: The Administrator offers experience and a proposed division of hours
sections.cue: Where did that guidance come from?
paragraphs: Congress had assigned courts responsibility for coverage decisions in individual suits, rather than creating an administrative tribunal to make the initial factual determinations. But the Administrator held enforcement and investigative powers and accumulated experience with industry practice. Interpretative Bulletin No. 13 and informal rulings told employers and employees how the public enforcement office understood the statute.

The Bulletin treated inactive-duty arrangements flexibly. Its examples included employees who had ample uninterrupted sleep and private time despite remaining continuously on call. Freedom to pursue personal activities and the length of consecutive idle periods were relevant.

For these employees, the Administrator would exclude sleeping and eating time because interruptions were rare and the men had adequate opportunity to do what they ordinarily would do privately. The Administrator would count the remaining on-call hours because the record did not show that their enjoyable uses were what the employees would have chosen without the employment restriction. That was the agency official’s proposed application, not a wage award by the Court.

sections.title: Administrative guidance earns weight through persuasion
sections.cue: Why was the agency view neither controlling nor irrelevant?
paragraphs: The interpretations did not result from adversarial administrative factfinding, and they did not bind trial courts as a superior court’s ruling would. Yet that absence did not make the guidance valueless. Specialized investigations could supply a wider base of information than a single lawsuit, and coordination between public enforcement and private litigation was desirable; divergent standards called for good reasons.

The Court treated the Administrator’s rulings, interpretations, and opinions as relevant experience and informed judgment. Their weight depended on the thoroughness of consideration, validity of reasoning, consistency with earlier and later positions, and other qualities making them persuasive. Substantial respect could follow from those qualities without giving the official authoritative control of the judicial decision.

sections.title: Reversal restores the factual question
sections.cue: What remained to be decided after the case returned?
paragraphs: On December 4, 1944, the Supreme Court reversed the Fifth Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion. Although the district court had mentioned the Bulletin, its legal assumption that waiting could not be work apparently restricted the inquiry. Removing that assumption allowed the required findings.

The Court did not decide that every nighttime hour was compensable, adopt the Administrator’s proposed allocation as binding, or calculate overtime, liquidated damages, or attorneys’ fees. The report contains no separate opinion or dissent notation. The necessary factual assessment remained for further proceedings.
